newsitem.title: USA: NYS reaches tentative pact to keep rent rules.
newsitem.headline: NYS reaches tentative pact to keep rent rules.

text.p: New York Gov. George Pataki said he reached a tentative agreement on apartment rent rules with Albany lawmakers that would save current rent rules for all but "a handful of millionaires."

The rent rules expired at midnight Sunday, and it will take a day or so for the Republican Senate, which had fought hard for much more sweeping changes, and the Democrat Assembly, which had wanted to preserve the current system, to act on the new bill, according to Monday's edition of The New York Times.

Pataki, in prepared remarks, said: "All tenants but a handful of millionaires are protected because I believe that we must not change the rent laws that so many people have counted on for years." The Republican governor had fought hard to let apartments be deregulated once tenants moved or died, but instead, a system of higher rent rises was agreed.
The last-minute compromise would make the following changes, according to the New York Times.

--Landlords may raise rents at least 20 percent on two-year leases after tenants move or die. Further raises will be allowed if the previous tenant occupied the apartment for eight years or more, or if very low rents--under $300--were charged for eight or more years.
--Apartments rented by tenants with an average household income of $175,000 per year for two years, and who pay at least $2,000 a month in rent, would be deregulated.
--Rent regulations would be extended for six more years.

--Tenants would no longer be allowed to will appartments to aunts, uncles, neices or nephews, and succession rights would be limited to one generation, though second-generation tenants could stay in an apartment if they paid a vacancy bounus.
